items.title: Census 2011 — Key Figures at a Glance
items.body:
**In one line:** Census 2011 is the big official head-count of India, and its headline numbers (population, density, sex ratio, literacy) are the raw material for almost every social-geography question.

**Why it is asked:** APPSC asks these figures directly ('India's population in 2011?') and uses them as options in statement questions, so the headline numbers must be at your fingertips.

## The story

A **census** is a complete count of every person in the country, done once every ten years (a **decennial** count). Census 2011 was the **15th** census of India and the **7th** since Independence. Counting began under **Lord Mayo in 1872** and became a regular ten-yearly exercise from **1881**; the first modern census anywhere was in Sweden (1749).

It was run by the **Registrar General and Census Commissioner (C. Chandramouli)** under the **Ministry of Home Affairs**, with the motto **'Our Census, Our Future'**. The work happened in **two phases** — **House-listing (April to September 2010)** and **Population Enumeration (9 to 28 February 2011)**.

## Picture it

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Total population | 121 crore (1,210,569,573) |
| Males / Females | 62.3 cr / 58.7 cr |
| Decadal growth (2001-11) | 17.7% (absolute +18.19 cr) |
| Density | 382 persons per sq km |
| Sex ratio (all ages) | 943 |
| Child sex ratio (0-6) | 919 |
| Literacy | 74.04% |
| Rural : Urban | 68.8% : 31.2% |
| SC / ST share | 16.6% / 8.6% |

Administrative spread: **640 districts, 5,924 sub-districts, 7,936 towns and about 6.4 lakh villages**.

**Density, work and faith (Census 2011)**
- **Density:** national density was **382 persons per sq km**, up from **325 in 2001**. Among states **Bihar** was the most densely populated (about 1,106); among Union Territories **Delhi** had the highest density.
- **Workforce:** the **primary sector** (agriculture and allied work) engaged about **54.6% of workers** — still the largest share.
- **Religion:** Hindus about **79.8%**, Muslims about **14.2%** (Islam is the largest minority religion), Christians about 2.3%.
- **Language:** Hindi is the most widely spoken scheduled language, followed by **Bengali**; the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution currently lists **22** scheduled languages.

**SC and ST shares** — Scheduled Castes form **16.6%** and Scheduled Tribes **8.6%** of India's population. **Punjab** has the highest SC share among states (about 31.9%), while **Nagaland** has effectively zero SC population.

## Terms explained

- **Census** — a full count of the whole population, taken every ten years.
- **Decennial** — happening once every ten years.
- **Decadal growth** — the percentage rise in population over the ten years since the last census.
- **Density** — the number of people living in each square kilometre.
- **Sex ratio** — the number of females for every 1000 males.

**Most and least urbanised (Census 2011)**
India was **31.2% urban**. Among states, **Goa** was the **most urbanised** (about 62%), and **Himachal Pradesh** the least (about 10%). Bihar and Assam were also among the least urbanised.

## Don't confuse

- **Sex ratio 943 is NOT the child sex ratio 919** — the first is for all ages, the second only for ages 0-6.
- **121 crore is the 2011 figure; 102 crore was 2001** — a common distractor.

## Remember it

The 'big four' of 2011: **121 - 382 - 943 - 74** = population 121 crore, density 382, sex ratio 943, literacy 74%.

## TL;DR

- Census 2011 = 15th census overall, 7th after Independence; began 1872 (Mayo), regular from 1881.
- Motto 'Our Census, Our Future'; Commissioner C. Chandramouli; under the Ministry of Home Affairs; two phases.
- Population 121 crore; density 382 per sq km; decadal growth 17.7% (+18.19 crore).
- Sex ratio 943, child sex ratio 919, literacy 74.04%; rural 68.8% : urban 31.2%; SC 16.6%, ST 8.6%.

items.title: Sex Ratio, Child Sex Ratio & Literacy
items.body:
**In one line:** This note explains two social-health scores — the sex ratio (how many girls per 1000 boys) and literacy (who can read and write) — and which states top and bottom each.

**Why it is asked:** State extremes (Kerala highest, Haryana lowest) and the falling child sex ratio are repeat one-mark and statement questions.

## The story

The **sex ratio** is the number of **females per 1000 males**. For all of India in 2011 it was **943** (up from 933 in 2001). Interestingly, the **rural ratio (949) is higher than the urban (929)**. **Kerala (1084)** tops the list and **Haryana** is lowest.

A separate, more worrying number is the **child sex ratio (0-6 years)**. It fell from **976 (1961) to 919 (2011)** — a sign that girls are 'missing' due to sex-selective practices. The worst is **Haryana (834)**. In the 1991-2001 decade the child ratio dropped below the overall ratio for the first time.

**Literacy** counts people aged **7 and above who can read and write with understanding**. India's literacy rose to **74.04%** in 2011 (from 64.83% in 2001), but with a wide **gender gap**: **male 82.14% versus female 65.46%** (a gap of 16.68 percentage points).

## Picture it

| Record | Highest | Lowest |
|---|---|---|
| Sex ratio (state) | Kerala 1084 | Haryana |
| Child sex ratio (0-6) | Arunachal 972 / Mizoram 970 | Haryana 834 |
| Literacy (state) | Kerala 94% | Bihar 61.8% |
| Literacy (district) | Serchhip (Mizoram) | Alirajpur (MP) |

Andhra Pradesh's sex ratio is **997** — above the national 943 and the **3rd-highest** after Kerala and Puducherry.

## Terms explained

- **Sex ratio** — females per 1000 males (all ages).
- **Child sex ratio** — females per 1000 males among children aged 0-6.
- **Literacy rate** — the share of people aged 7+ who can read and write with understanding.
- **Gender gap** — the difference between male and female literacy.

## Don't confuse

- **Sex ratio (943) versus child sex ratio (919)** — do not swap the all-age and 0-6 figures.
- **Haryana is lowest for BOTH sex ratio and child sex ratio** — a frequent trap pairs Haryana with 'highest'.

## Remember it

'**Kerala tops, Haryana bottoms**' for both sex ratio and literacy direction; the child ratio is the falling warning sign (976 down to 919).

## TL;DR

- Sex ratio 943 (rural 949 > urban 929); highest Kerala 1084, lowest Haryana; AP 997.
- Child sex ratio (0-6) declined from 976 (1961) to 919 (2011); lowest Haryana (834).
- Literacy 74.04% — male 82.14%, female 65.46%, gender gap 16.68 percentage points.
- Highest literacy Kerala (94%), lowest Bihar (61.8%); SC 66.1%, ST 59%.
- In 1991-2001 the child sex ratio fell below the overall sex ratio for the first time.

items.title: Population Growth, Age Structure & Demographic Transition
items.body:
**In one line:** This note tracks how fast India's population has grown over the decades, how its age mix is changing, and the standard theory (demographic transition) that explains why.

**Why it is asked:** The 'only negative-growth decade', the 'maximum-growth decade' and the three transition stages are classic one-mark facts; the demographic dividend links to Mains.

## The story

India's growth has not been steady. The decade **1911-1921** was the **only one with negative growth (-0.03%)**, because the 1918-19 influenza epidemic killed millions. The year **1921** is called the **'Great Divide'** — after it, death rates began to fall and population climbed. Growth peaked in **1961-1971 (24.8%)**, and the stretch **1951-1981** is called the **'population explosion'**. Since 1981 the growth rate has been falling; it was **17.7%** in 2001-2011.

Meanwhile the **age structure** changed. The share of children (0-14) fell from **42% (1971) to 29% (2011)**, while the **working-age group (15-59) rose to 63%** and the elderly (60+) to about 8%. A large working-age group relative to dependants is the **demographic dividend** — a chance for faster economic growth.

The **Demographic Transition Theory** describes this journey in stages, driven by falling birth and death rates.

## Picture it

| Stage | Birth rate | Death rate | Growth |
|---|---|---|---|
| I | High | High | Low / stagnant |
| II | High | Falling | Rapid (explosion) |
| III | Low | Low | Low / stable |

India is broadly in **late Stage II / early Stage III**, with fertility near the replacement level (2.1) in many states.

## Terms explained

- **Decadal growth** — the percentage change in population over ten years.
- **Age structure** — how the population splits into children, working-age adults and the elderly.
- **Demographic dividend** — the growth opportunity when the working-age share is large and dependants are few.
- **Replacement-level fertility** — about 2.1 children per woman, the level that keeps a population steady.
- **Demographic transition** — the shift from high birth-and-death rates to low birth-and-death rates as a country develops.

- **Crude Birth Rate (CBR)** — live births per 1,000 population in a year.
- **Total Fertility Rate (TFR)** — the average number of children a woman would have over her lifetime; about 2.1 is replacement level.
- **Infant Mortality Rate (IMR)** — deaths of infants under 1 year per 1,000 live births.

## Don't confuse

- **Negative growth was 1911-1921, not 1921-1931** — a common swap.
- **Maximum growth was 1961-1971**, while the 'explosion' spans the longer 1951-1981.
- **The dividend is about the working-age bulge, not the elderly.**

## Remember it

Growth extremes: '**Negative 1911-21, Maximum 1961-71**'. Transition: high-high, high-falling, low-low.

## TL;DR

- 1911-1921 was the only decade of negative growth (influenza epidemic); 1921 = the 'Great Divide'.
- 1961-1971 saw maximum decadal growth (24.8%); 1951-1981 = the population explosion.
- 0-14 share fell 42% (1971) to 29% (2011); 15-59 rose to 63% — the basis of the demographic dividend.
- Demographic Transition: Stage I high birth/death, Stage II falling death (rapid growth), Stage III low/stable.
- Malthus argued population grows geometrically while food grows arithmetically.

items.title: Migration, Distribution & Settlement Patterns
items.body:
**In one line:** This note covers why and how people move (migration), where they end up living (distribution and density), and the shapes their villages and towns take (settlements).

**Why it is asked:** 'Largest migration stream', the push-pull idea, and the urban hierarchy (metropolis versus megacity) are frequent one-mark and match questions.

## The story

**Migration** is the movement of people from one place to another to live. Within India there are four **streams**: **rural-to-rural (the largest, mostly women moving on marriage)**, rural-to-urban, urban-to-urban and urban-to-rural. People leave for **push factors** (unemployment, poverty, disasters, unrest) and are drawn by **pull factors** (jobs, security, better services). Marriage is the leading reason women migrate; work is the leading reason men do.

Where people settle is uneven: worldwide **over 90% of people live on about 10% of the land**. What decides this is a mix of **geographical** (water, flat land, climate, soils), **economic** (minerals, industry, towns) and **socio-cultural** factors.

A **settlement** is a place where people live. **Rural settlements** take shapes such as **nucleated (clustered), dispersed (scattered), semi-clustered and hamleted**. **Urban settlements** climb a ladder of size — the **urban hierarchy**.

## Picture it

| Urban rank | Size |
|---|---|
| Class-I town | 1 lakh (100,000) or more |
| Million-plus city | over 10 lakh |
| Metropolis | over 1 million |
| Megacity | over 10 million |

## Terms explained

- **Migration** — moving from one place to another to live.
- **Push factor** — something that drives people away (joblessness, disaster).
- **Pull factor** — something that attracts people in (jobs, services).
- **Net Migration Rate** — immigrants minus emigrants, per 1000 people.
- **Nucleated settlement** — houses clustered tightly together (opposite of dispersed/scattered).
- **Megacity** — an urban area of more than 10 million people.

## Don't confuse

- **Rural-to-rural is the largest stream, not rural-to-urban** — the latter grabs headlines but is smaller.
- **Nucleated means clustered; dispersed means scattered** — do not reverse them.
- **Metropolis (over 1 million) is smaller than a megacity (over 10 million).**

## Remember it

Streams: '**R-R biggest, marriage moves women, work moves men**'; cities: 'metro = 1 million, mega = 10 million'.

## TL;DR

- Internal migration streams: rural-rural (largest), rural-urban, urban-urban, urban-rural.
- Push = unemployment / disasters / unrest; Pull = jobs / security / services; marriage drives female migration.
- Over 90% of the world's people live on about 10% of the land.
- Rural settlement types: nucleated, dispersed, semi-clustered, hamleted.
- Urban hierarchy: metropolis over 1 million, megacity over 10 million; a Class-I town has 1 lakh or more.

items.title: Tribes of India & Andhra Pradesh (incl. PVTGs)
items.body:
**In one line:** This note explains who Scheduled Tribes are, the special sub-group called PVTGs (the most vulnerable tribes), and which tribes belong to India and to Andhra Pradesh.

**Why it is asked:** 'How many PVTGs', 'Chenchu belongs to which state', and AP's largest tribe are recurring APPSC facts, often as match-the-following.

## The story

**Scheduled Tribes (ST)** are communities listed in the Constitution for special protection; they are **8.6%** of India (2011). The states with the **highest ST share** are Mizoram and Nagaland, while **Madhya Pradesh** has the **largest ST numbers**. India's biggest individual tribes are the **Gond, Bhil and Santhal**.

Among the STs, some are especially disadvantaged and are called **Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs)**. India has **75 PVTGs** across **18 states and 1 Union Territory**. They are picked using four tests: **pre-agricultural technology, very low literacy, a stagnant or falling population, and geographical isolation**.

In **Andhra Pradesh** (undivided), there were **12 PVTGs**. The best-known is the **Chenchu** of the **Nallamala forests (within the Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve)**. Others include **Konda Reddi, Konda Savara, Bodo and Gutob Gadaba, Dongria and Kutia Khond, Bondo and Khond Porja, Kolam and Thoti**. AP's **largest** Scheduled Tribe overall is the **Yanadi** of the Nellore region. Tribes cluster in the **Eastern Ghats agency areas** (Alluri Sitharama Raju, Parvathipuram Manyam) and the Nallamala hills.

## Picture it

| Level | Fact |
|---|---|
| ST share of India (2011) | 8.6% |
| Largest tribes of India | Gond, Bhil, Santhal |
| PVTGs in India | 75 (18 states + 1 UT) |
| Best-known AP PVTG | Chenchu (Nallamala) |
| Largest AP Scheduled Tribe | Yanadi (Nellore) |

**Where AP's tribes live**

| Tribe | Habitat |
|---|---|
| Chenchu (PVTG) | Nallamala forests (Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam) |
| Konda Reddi (PVTG) | Godavari / Papikonda hills |
| Yanadi (largest ST) | Nellore coastal plains |
| Konda Savara (PVTG) | Srikakulam / north-coastal Eastern Ghats |

## Terms explained

- **Scheduled Tribe (ST)** — a tribal community listed in the Constitution for special support.
- **PVTG** — Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, the most disadvantaged STs.
- **Agency area** — a Scheduled Area with tribal self-governance protections, mostly in the Eastern Ghats.
- **Pre-agricultural technology** — relying on hunting, gathering or shifting cultivation rather than settled farming.

## Don't confuse

- **Chenchu is a PVTG of the Nallamala (AP-Telangana), not a Nilgiri or Odisha tribe.**
- **Yanadi is AP's largest ST; the Chenchu, though famous, are a small PVTG.**
- **75 PVTGs across 18 states + 1 UT** — not '18 PVTGs'.

## Remember it

AP tribal headline: '**Yanadi biggest, Chenchu most famous (Nallamala)**'; India has **75 PVTGs**.

## TL;DR

- ST = 8.6% of India (2011); Gond, Bhil and Santhal are the largest tribes.
- India has 75 PVTGs across 18 states and 1 UT, chosen on four vulnerability tests.
- Chenchu is the best-known PVTG of Andhra Pradesh (Nallamala / Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam).
- Undivided AP had 12 PVTGs incl. Chenchu, Konda Reddi, Konda Savara, Bodo/Gutob Gadaba, Dongria/Kutia Khond, Bondo/Khond Porja, Kolam, Thoti.
- Yanadi is AP's largest Scheduled Tribe (Nellore region); tribes concentrate in the Eastern Ghats and Nallamala.

items.title: AP Demographics, Population Policy & the 2027 Census
items.body:
**In one line:** This note gives Andhra Pradesh's own population figures, India's family-planning policy, and the key features of the next count — Census 2027.

**Why it is asked:** AP's sex ratio and literacy versus the national average, the NPP 2000 target, and 'Census 2027 firsts' (digital, caste count) are current and recurring APPSC points.

## The story

For **Andhra Pradesh** (residuary state, Census 2011), the population was about **4.94 crore** — roughly **4.08%** of India and the **10th** most populous state. Its **sex ratio is 997**, well above the national 943 and among the best in the country; its **density is about 304 per sq km**, below the national 382; and its **literacy (about 67%)** is below the national 74%. SC are about 17% and ST about 5.5%.

On **policy**, India was the **first country in the world** to adopt an official family-planning programme (**1952**). The **National Population Policy 2000** set the goal of **replacement-level fertility (a TFR of 2.1)** and population stabilisation by 2045, backed by later measures such as Mission Parivar Vikas, Beti Bachao Beti Padhao and the PCPNDT Act (1994).

The next count, **Census 2027**, is the **16th** census and India's **first fully digital** one, with **optional self-enumeration** (in 16 languages) and **caste enumeration** for the first time since 1931. It will feed the next **delimitation** (re-drawing of constituency boundaries).

## Picture it

| AP (Census 2011) | Value |
|---|---|
| Population | about 4.94 crore (10th) |
| Sex ratio | 997 (above national 943) |
| Density | about 304 per sq km (below national 382) |
| Literacy | about 67% (below national 74%) |

Census 2027 phases: **House-listing April-September 2026**; **Population Enumeration 9-28 February 2027** (reference date 1 March 2027; snow-bound regions enumerated September 2026 with reference 1 October 2026).

**More AP numbers (Census 2011)** — decadal growth 2001-2011 was about **9.2%**, below the national **17.7%**; Scheduled Castes were about **17.1%** and Scheduled Tribes about **5.5%** of the population (so SCs formed a larger share than STs); the urban share was about **29.6%**, below the national urban share of 31.2%.

**AP in NFHS-5 (2019-21)** — Total Fertility Rate **1.7**, below the replacement level of 2.1; institutional births very high (about **97%**); the sex ratio of the total population was **above 1000** females per 1000 males (about 1,045).

**India in the world** — according to UN estimates, in **2023 India surpassed China** to become the world's most populous country, crossing about **1.43 billion**; India holds roughly **one-sixth (about 17-18%)** of the world's population.

## Terms explained

- **Residuary state** — what remained of Andhra Pradesh after Telangana was carved out in 2014.
- **Replacement-level fertility** — a TFR of about 2.1, which keeps a population steady.
- **Self-enumeration** — people filling in their own census details online.
- **Delimitation** — redrawing the boundaries of electoral constituencies based on population.

**The top four countries by population (UN, 2023 onward)**

| Rank | Country |
|---|---|
| Most populous (1st) | India (since 2023) |
| Second most populous | China |
| Third most populous | United States |
| Fourth most populous | Indonesia |

## Don't confuse

- **AP's sex ratio (997) is ABOVE the national 943**, but its literacy (67%) is BELOW the national 74%.
- **The family-planning programme began in 1952; the current policy is NPP 2000** — not 1976.
- **Caste enumeration returns after 1931**, not after 2011.

## Remember it

AP: '**high sex ratio, low literacy**'; Census 2027: '**16th, first digital, caste count back after 1931**'.

## TL;DR

- AP (2011, residuary): population about 4.94 crore, sex ratio 997 (above national), density about 304, literacy about 67%.
- India was the first country to adopt an official family-planning policy (1952).
- National Population Policy 2000 targets replacement-level fertility (TFR 2.1).
- Census 2027 is the 16th census, India's first digital census, with caste enumeration (first since 1931).
- Census 2027 reference date is 1 March 2027 (1 October 2026 for snow-bound regions); it feeds delimitation.

items.title: World Regional Geography — Canals, Isthmuses, Rivers, Lakes, Capitals & Peoples
items.body:
**In one line:** This is a quick-reference note for world geography trivia that APPSC repeats — ship canals, isthmuses, rivers and their capital cities, famous lakes, tricky capitals and the world's peoples.

**Why it is asked:** These facts appear as straight one-mark questions and as match-the-following options; they are easy marks if memorised.

## The story

A **canal** is a man-made waterway and an **isthmus** is a narrow neck of land joining two larger landmasses. The two great ship canals are the **Suez** (1869, Mediterranean to Red Sea, no locks) and the **Panama** (1914, Atlantic to Pacific, using locks). Many capital cities grew on **rivers**, and a handful of **lakes** hold world records. Finally, several **peoples** are tied to particular climates and deserts.

## Picture it

| Canal / isthmus | Links / location |
|---|---|
| Suez Canal (1869) | Mediterranean-Red Sea; Egypt; no locks |
| Panama Canal (1914) | Atlantic-Pacific; uses locks |
| Kiel Canal | North Sea-Baltic Sea; Germany |
| Isthmus of Panama | joins North and South America |
| Isthmus of Suez | joins Africa and Asia |
| Isthmus of Kra | Malay Peninsula (Thailand) |

| River | Capital(s) on it |
|---|---|
| Thames | London |
| Seine | Paris |
| Tiber | Rome |
| Danube (Europe's second-longest river, after the Volga) | Vienna, Budapest, Belgrade |
| Nile | Cairo |
| Tigris | Baghdad |
| Potomac | Washington D.C. |

| Lake | Record |
|---|---|
| Caspian Sea | Largest lake by area |
| Superior | Largest freshwater lake by area |
| Baikal | Deepest; largest by volume |
| Victoria | Largest in Africa |
| Titicaca | Highest navigable |
| Dead Sea | Lowest; among the saltiest |

| People | Region |
|---|---|
| Kirghiz | Central Asian steppes |
| Maori | New Zealand |
| Lapps (Sami) | Arctic Scandinavia |
| Tuareg | Sahara Desert |
| Mongols | Gobi Desert |
| Eskimo (Inuit) | Arctic tundra |
| Bushmen (San) | Kalahari Desert |
| Pygmies | Congo basin rainforest |
| Masai | East African savanna (Kenya/Tanzania) |
| Bedouin | Arabian deserts |
| Bindibu and Aborigines | Australian deserts (hunter-gatherers) |

**Natural regions and grasslands**

| Region | What it is |
|---|---|
| Equatorial (Selva) | dense evergreen tropical rainforest with no dry season |
| Savanna | tropical grassland with scattered trees and a wet-dry regime |
| Taiga | northern coniferous (boreal) forest belt |
| Tundra | treeless cold region of mosses and lichens |

Temperate grasslands are almost treeless: **Prairies** (North America), **Pampas** (Argentina/Uruguay), **Steppes** (Central Eurasia), **Veld** (South Africa), **Downs** (Australia). Their local winds are famous too: the **Chinook** is a warm, dry wind of the North American Prairies; the **Mistral** a cold wind of the Rhone valley.

**Straits and channels**

| Strait | Links / separates |
|---|---|
| Palk Strait | India and Sri Lanka |
| Strait of Malacca | Andaman Sea and South China Sea |
| Bering Strait | Asia and North America |
| Strait of Hormuz | Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman |
| Ten Degree Channel | separates the Andaman Islands from the Nicobar Islands |

**Continents and countries** — Asia is the most populous continent; Africa has the largest number of countries (54). Australia is both a country and the smallest continent. By area the largest countries are **Russia** and **Canada**, then the **USA and China** (so close that sources rank them 3rd/4th differently); India is 7th.

## Terms explained

- **Canal** — a man-made channel of water for ships or irrigation.
- **Isthmus** — a narrow strip of land joining two larger landmasses.
- **Lock** — a water-filled chamber that raises or lowers ships between different water levels (Panama uses them; Suez does not).
- **Navigable lake** — one deep and large enough for boats to sail on.

## Don't confuse

- **Suez has no locks; Panama uses locks** — a classic distractor pair.
- **Capitals, not biggest cities:** Canberra (not Sydney), Ottawa (not Toronto), Brasilia (not Rio), Ankara (not Istanbul).
- **Titicaca is in South America (highest navigable), not Africa; Victoria is Africa's largest.**

## Remember it

'**Suez no-locks, Panama locks**'; '**Caspian biggest, Baikal deepest**'.

## TL;DR

- Suez (Mediterranean-Red Sea, no locks) and Panama (Atlantic-Pacific, with locks) are the key ship canals; Kiel links the North Sea and Baltic.
- Capitals on rivers: London-Thames, Paris-Seine, Cairo-Nile, Baghdad-Tigris, Rome-Tiber.
- Caspian = largest lake; Baikal = deepest; Superior = largest freshwater by area; Victoria = largest in Africa; Titicaca = highest navigable.
- Non-obvious capitals: Canberra, Ottawa, Brasilia, Ankara.
- Peoples: Kirghiz (steppes), Maori (New Zealand), Lapps/Sami (Arctic), Tuareg (Sahara), Mongols (Gobi).

items.title: Tribe–State Mapping (All-India, UPSC-style)
items.body:
**In one line:** This is a focused match-the-following note that pins each commonly-tested tribe to its home state, with the traps the exam loves.

**Why it is asked:** Prelims regularly gives a List-I of tribes and a List-II of states; one or two deliberately wrong pairings decide the answer.

## The story

Tribes are tied to specific regions, and the exam tests whether you can place each one correctly. The two classic traps are putting the **Karbi** in Himachal Pradesh (they are of **Assam**) and the **Bonda** in Tamil Nadu (they are of **Odisha**). Learn the table below and these questions become free marks.

## Picture it

| Tribe | State / Region |
|---|---|
| Limboo (Limbu) | Sikkim |
| Dongaria Kondh (PVTG) | Odisha (Niyamgiri hills) |
| Karbi | Assam (NOT Himachal Pradesh) |
| Bonda (PVTG) | Odisha — Malkangiri hills (NOT Tamil Nadu) |
| Bhotia / Lepcha | Sikkim-north Bengal |
| Toda | Nilgiris, Tamil Nadu |
| Gond | Central India (largely Madhya Pradesh); among India's largest tribes |
| Santhal | Chota Nagpur region (Jharkhand/West Bengal) |
| Chenchu (PVTG) | Andhra Pradesh-Telangana (Nallamala) |

## Terms explained

- **PVTG** — Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group, the most disadvantaged Scheduled Tribes.
- **Niyamgiri** — the Odisha hill range that is home to the Dongaria Kondh.
- **Nilgiris** — the 'Blue Mountains' of Tamil Nadu, home of the Toda.

## Don't confuse

- **Karbi = Assam, NOT Himachal Pradesh.**
- **Bonda = Odisha, NOT Tamil Nadu.**
- **Toda = Nilgiris (Tamil Nadu); do not mix with the Chenchu of the Nallamala.**

## Remember it

Trap-busters: '**Karbi-Assam, Bonda-Odisha, Limboo-Sikkim**'.

## TL;DR

- Limboo (Limbu) is a tribe of Sikkim.
- Dongaria Kondh (a PVTG) live in the Niyamgiri hills of Odisha.
- Karbi are of Assam, not Himachal Pradesh.
- Bonda (a PVTG) are of Odisha, not Tamil Nadu.
- Chenchu (PVTG) belong to the Nallamala region of Andhra Pradesh-Telangana.

items.title: Census in India — History, Administration and Census 2027
items.body:
### Census in India — History, Administration and Census 2027

**In one line**
India's census is a decennial count run under the **Census Act, 1948**; exam items ask who started it, when it became synchronous, and what is new in Census 2027.

**The story**
The first city census was of **Dhaka** in 1830 by **Henry Walter**, called the father of census in India. The first all-India count (non-synchronous) came in **1872** under Lord **Mayo**; the first synchronous decennial census in **1881** under Lord **Ripon** (Census Commissioner W.C. Plowden). The first modern census anywhere was **Sweden** in **1749**. Today the Registrar General and Census Commissioner (Ministry of Home Affairs) runs it under the Census Act, 1948. Census 2011 covered 35 States/UTs, 640 districts, **5,924** sub-districts, **7,936** towns (**4,041** statutory + **3,894** census towns) and about 6.41 lakh villages. The **National Population Register** was first prepared with the 2010 house-listing. Caste was last fully counted in **1931**; the **SECC** 2011 was a separate survey.

**Census 2027** — Census 2021 was **postponed** (COVID-19). The new count is the 16th census and the **8th since Independence**. The **house-listing** phase runs April–September 2026 (each state picks a **30-day** window); enumeration is in February 2027 with reference date 1 March 2027, but for **snow-bound** Ladakh, J&K, Himachal and Uttarakhand the reference date is **1 October 2026**. Enumerators collect data on **mobile apps**, with an online self-enumeration option, and caste is counted for the first time since 1931.

**Don't confuse**
1872 (Mayo) = first, non-synchronous; 1881 (Ripon) = first synchronous. Statutory towns are notified by law; census towns qualify by population, density and non-farm work.

**TL;DR**
- Dhaka 1830 (Henry Walter); 1872 Mayo; 1881 Ripon (synchronous); Census Act 1948; RGI under MHA.
- 2011: 35 States/UTs, 640 districts, 7,936 towns (4,041 statutory, 3,894 census).
- Census 2027: 16th, 8th since Independence; house-listing Apr–Sep 2026; reference 1 Mar 2027 (1 Oct 2026 snow-bound); digital, caste.
keyPoints: Henry Walter conducted the first city census (Dhaka, 1830) and is called the father of census in India.
The first all-India census was in 1872 (Lord Mayo); the first synchronous decennial census in 1881 (Lord Ripon).
The census is conducted under the Census Act, 1948 by the Registrar General, Ministry of Home Affairs.
Census 2011 counted 7,936 towns: 4,041 statutory and 3,894 census towns.
Census 2027 is the 16th census (8th since Independence); snow-bound areas use the reference date 1 October 2026.

items.body:
### Census 2011 Records — States, UTs and Districts

**In one line**
Census 2011 records are the most-asked social-geography facts: which state or UT tops or bottoms each measure.

**The story**
India held about **17.5**% of the world's people on 2.4% of its land. The final count was 1,210,854,977 (**121.09** crore). Decadal growth fell from **21.5**% (1991–2001) to 17.7% — the sharpest fall since Independence. Literacy rose by **9.21** points; a literate is a person aged 7+ who reads and writes with understanding, and the **effective literacy** rate leaves out children aged 0–6.

| Measure | Record (Census 2011) |
|---|---|
| Most populous state | **Uttar Pradesh** (~19.98 crore, **16.5**%) |
| Least populous state / UT | **Sikkim** / **Lakshadweep** |
| Next most populous | **Maharashtra**, Bihar, **West Bengal**, MP |
| Share of world | **17.5**% of people on 2.4% of land |
| Least dense state / UT | Arunachal Pradesh (**17 per** km²) / A&N (**46**) |
| Densest UT / district | Delhi (**11,320**) / North-East Delhi (~37,346) |
| Densest states | Bihar (**1,106**), West Bengal (**1,028**) |
| Highest growth 2001–11 | **Meghalaya** (**27.9**%), then Arunachal, Bihar; UT Dadra & Nagar Haveli 55.9% |
| Lowest growth 2001–11 | **Nagaland** (**negative**, −0.6%); Kerala lowest positive (4.9%) |
| Sex ratio — UTs | highest Puducherry (**1,037**), lowest Daman & Diu (**618**) |
| Sex ratio — lowest state | Haryana (**879**) |
| Sex ratio — districts | **Mahe** (**1,184**) highest; Daman (533) lowest |
| Child sex ratio — highest | Arunachal Pradesh (**972**), Mizoram and Meghalaya (970) |
| Child sex ratio — lowest | Haryana (**834**), Punjab (**846**) |
| Top literacy | Kerala 94, Lakshadweep **91.8**, Mizoram **91.3**, Goa 88.7, Tripura 87.2 |
| Lowest literacy | Bihar 61.8, Arunachal **65.4**, **Rajasthan** 66.1 |
| Female literacy | highest Kerala (~92%), lowest Rajasthan (~**52**%) |
| Literacy definition | aged 7+, reads and writes with understanding; **effective literacy** excludes 0–6 |
| Literacy gain | 64.83% → 74.04% (+**9.21** points) |
| Urban / rural population (absolute) | Maharashtra has the **largest urban population**; UP the largest rural |
| Urbanisation extremes | Delhi **97.5**%; HP 10%, Bihar **11.3**% |
| Rural share | Himachal Pradesh has the **highest share of rural** population (~90%) |
| Million-plus UAs | **53**, led by **Greater Mumbai**, Delhi, Kolkata |
| Class-I cities | **468** |
| Work participation | **39.8**% (male 53.3, female **25.5**) |
| Worker categories | **agricultural labourers** 30% > **cultivators** 24.6% (first time) |
| Age groups | 0–14 30.8%, 15–59 **60.3**%, 60+ 8.6% (**10.4 crore**) |
| Final count | 1,210,854,977 (**121.09** crore) |
| Growth slowdown | **21.5**% (1991–2001) → 17.7% (2001–11) |

**Don't confuse**
Haryana: lowest sex ratio (879) AND lowest child sex ratio (834). Arunachal: highest child sex ratio (972) but least dense (17). Meghalaya = highest growth; Nagaland = negative growth. Goa = most urbanised state; Maharashtra = largest urban population.

**TL;DR**
- Population: UP (16.5%) > Maharashtra > Bihar > WB > MP; Sikkim least; India 17.5% of world.
- Density: Bihar 1,106, WB 1,028; Delhi 11,320; Arunachal 17; A&N 46.
- Sex ratio: Haryana 879; Puducherry 1,037, Daman & Diu 618; CSR Arunachal 972, Haryana 834.
- Literacy: Kerala, Lakshadweep, Mizoram top; Bihar, Arunachal, Rajasthan bottom; female lowest Rajasthan.
- Growth: Meghalaya 27.9% top; Nagaland negative; WPR 39.8%; agri labourers > cultivators.
keyPoints: Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state (16.5% of India); Sikkim the least populous.
Bihar (1,106/km²) is the densest state and Arunachal Pradesh (17/km²) the least dense.
Meghalaya had the highest decadal growth (27.9%) and Nagaland negative growth in 2001–11.
Haryana had the lowest sex ratio (879) and child sex ratio (834); Arunachal the highest child sex ratio (972).
In 2011 agricultural labourers (30%) outnumbered cultivators (24.6%) for the first time.

### SC/ST Distribution, Religion and Language (Census 2011)

**In one line**
Who has the most SCs and STs (by share and by number), which states have none, and how religion and language split the population.

**The story**
Scheduled Castes are 16.6% and Scheduled Tribes 8.6% of India. Shares and numbers rank differently: Punjab has the highest SC **share**, but Uttar Pradesh the **largest SC population**; Mizoram has the highest ST share among states, but Madhya Pradesh the most STs. Literacy was **66.1**% among SCs and **59**% among STs. Census 2011 recorded **121 languages** spoken by 10,000 or more — 22 scheduled and **99** non-scheduled. **Santhali** (**Ol Chiki** script), Bodo, Maithili and Dogri joined the Eighth Schedule in 2003 (**92nd** Amendment).

| Measure | Fact |
|---|---|
| Highest SC share | Punjab 31.9%, Himachal **25.2**%, West Bengal **23.5**% |
| Largest SC number | **Uttar Pradesh** (**largest SC population**) |
| No SC population | Nagaland, A&N, Lakshadweep (**no Scheduled Caste**) |
| Highest ST share | Lakshadweep **94.8**%; Mizoram **94.4**%, Nagaland, Meghalaya |
| Largest ST number | **Madhya Pradesh** (~**1.53 crore**), Maharashtra, Odisha |
| No ST population | Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh, Delhi, Puducherry (**no notified Scheduled Tribes**) |
| SC / ST literacy | **66.1**% / **59**% |
| Religion shares | Hindus 79.8, Muslims 14.2, Christians 2.3, Sikhs **1.7**, Buddhists **0.7**, Jains 0.4 (%) |
| Religious growth 2001–11 | Hindus 16.8%, Muslims **24.6**%, Christians 15.5%, Sikhs 8.4%, Jains **5.4**% |
| Majority religion | Nagaland, Mizoram, Meghalaya **Christian-majority**; Punjab **Sikh-majority**; J&K, Lakshadweep Muslim-majority |
| Buddhists and Jains | Maharashtra has the largest **Buddhist** and Jain populations |
| Mother tongues | Hindi 43.6, Bengali 8.0, Marathi 6.9, **Telugu** 6.7 (**fourth**; third in 2001), Tamil 5.7 (%) |

**Don't confuse**
Share vs number: SC share Punjab, SC number UP; ST share Mizoram (Lakshadweep among UTs), ST number MP. Telugu is the 4th most spoken language (it was 3rd in 2001).

**TL;DR**
- SC: Punjab 31.9 > HP 25.2 > WB 23.5 (share); UP (number); none in Nagaland, A&N, Lakshadweep.
- ST: Lakshadweep 94.8, Mizoram 94.4 (share); MP 1.53 cr (number); none in Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Chandigarh, Puducherry.
- Religion: 79.8/14.2/2.3/1.7/0.7/0.4; Language: Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Telugu (4th), Tamil.

Mizoram (94.4%) has the highest ST share among states; Madhya Pradesh the largest ST population.
Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh, Delhi and Puducherry have no notified Scheduled Tribes.
Telugu was the fourth most spoken language in 2011 (after Hindi, Bengali and Marathi).

items.title: Demographic Measures, Transition, NFHS-5 and World Population
items.body:
### Demographic Measures, Transition, NFHS-5 and World Population

**In one line**
Population questions test definitions (dependency ratio, MMR, NRR), the transition model, the latest survey numbers and India's policy targets.

**The story**
The **dependency ratio** counts children (0–14) and the elderly per 100 working-age people; a falling ratio opens the demographic-dividend window, which for India is expected to last until about **2055**–56. **Notestein**'s transition model runs from high stationary through early and late expanding to **low stationary** (and, in some versions, declining). Population pyramids show the same story — **expansive** (wide base, high births), **constrictive** (narrow base, ageing) and stationary. MMR counts maternal deaths per **1,00,000** live births; IMR per 1,000. A **Net Reproduction Rate** of 1 means mothers exactly replace themselves; **Optimum population** is the size giving the highest per-capita output. **Malthus** proposed **positive checks** (famine, disease, war) and **preventive checks** (late marriage, restraint).

**Latest numbers:** **NFHS-5** (2019–21) put India's TFR at **2.0**; it recorded **1,020** women per 1,000 men — the first time women outnumbered men in an NFHS — and a sex ratio at birth of **929**. World population crossed **8 billion** on 15 November 2022; UNFPA's 2025 report put India at about **146.4** crore with a TFR of **1.9**; UN projections see India peaking at about **1.7 billion** in the early 2060s. Asia holds about **60%** of humanity; **Monaco** is the densest country.

**Policy:** family planning began in 1952 and the first National Population Policy came in **1976**. NPP 2000 has an immediate aim, a **medium-term** aim (TFR 2.1 by 2010) and a long-term aim of a stable population by **2045**; the **National Commission on Population** (2000) is chaired by the Prime Minister.

**Don't confuse**
NFHS-5 TFR 2.0 (India) vs AP 1.7; NFHS sex ratio 1,020 (survey, household) vs Census 2011 943 (count). MMR is per lakh, IMR per thousand.

**TL;DR**
- Dependency ratio; dividend window to ~2055; Notestein stages; pyramids expansive/constrictive/stationary.
- NFHS-5: TFR 2.0, sex ratio 1,020, SRB 929; world 8 bn (15 Nov 2022); UNFPA 2025 India 146.4 cr, TFR 1.9.
- Policies: 1952 programme, 1976 first NPP, NPP 2000 (stability by 2045).
keyPoints: The dependency ratio relates children and the elderly to the working-age population.
NFHS-5 (2019–21): India's TFR 2.0; 1,020 women per 1,000 men; sex ratio at birth 929.
World population crossed 8 billion on 15 November 2022.
NPP 2000 aims at a stable population by 2045; the first National Population Policy came in 1976.
Malthus distinguished positive checks from preventive checks.

items.title: Migration — Theory, Data and Remittances
items.body:
### Migration — Theory, Data and Remittances

**In one line**
Migration questions ask who framed migration theory, how Census measures migrants, and India's migration records.

**The story**
**Ravenstein**'s "laws of migration" (**1885**) say most migrants move short distances and long-distance migrants head to big cities, with women dominating short-distance moves. **Everett Lee** (1966) explained migration by factors at origin and destination, **intervening obstacles** and personal factors — the push–pull model. Census 2011 counted about **45.6 crore** migrants by place of last residence (about 37%). Migration may be internal or international; permanent, seasonal or **circular**; voluntary or forced. **Transhumance** is the seasonal up-and-down movement of herders such as the Gaddis, **Bakarwal**s and Bhotias.

Maharashtra and Delhi receive the largest **net in-migration**; UP and Bihar send the most out-migrants. India is the world's **largest recipient** of **remittances** (about US$129 billion in 2024) and has the largest **diaspora** (over 3 crore). Emigration of the skilled is **brain drain**.

**Don't confuse**
Ravenstein = laws (1885); Lee = push–pull with intervening obstacles (1966). Transhumance is seasonal and returns; nomadism has no fixed base.

**TL;DR**
- Ravenstein 1885; Everett Lee 1966.
- 45.6 crore migrants (2011); rural–rural largest stream; Maharashtra/Delhi top destinations.
- Transhumance: Gaddi, Bakarwal, Bhotia; India largest remittance receiver.
keyPoints: Ravenstein formulated the laws of migration in 1885.
Everett Lee's model adds intervening obstacles and personal factors to push and pull.
Transhumance is the seasonal movement of herders such as the Gaddis and Bakarwals.
India is the world's largest recipient of remittances.

items.title: Settlements — Rural Types, Town Definitions, Functional Towns and Urban Theories
items.body:
### Settlements — Rural Types, Town Definitions, Functional Towns and Urban Theories

**In one line**
Settlement questions match a type to its region, a town to its function, or an urban term to the geographer who coined it.

**The story**
Rural settlements are **Compact** (clustered) in fertile plains, **Semi-clustered** where a compact village fragments, hamleted where the village splits into units (**panna**, para, palli, nagla, **dhani**), and **Dispersed** in hills and forests. Shapes vary — linear, rectangular, circular, **star-like**, **T-shaped**, double and cross-shaped. Urban places are either statutory towns (municipality, corporation, **cantonment board**, notified area) or census towns (≥5,000 people, density ≥**400**/km², ≥**75%** of male main workers non-farm). An urban agglomeration is a town with its **outgrowths**. Census size classes run from Class I (1 lakh+) through Class II (**50,000**+) down to **Class VI** (below 5,000).

| Settlement / term | Region / meaning |
|---|---|
| **Compact** / nucleated | fertile plains — **Punjab**–Haryana–W UP; for security and shared land |
| **Semi-clustered** | Gujarat plains, parts of Rajasthan |
| Hamleted | units called **panna**, para, palli, nagla, **dhani**; middle–lower Ganga plain, Chhattisgarh |
| **Dispersed** / isolated | **Meghalaya**, Uttarakhand, Himachal, Kerala |
| Shapes | linear, rectangular, circular, **star-like**, **T-shaped**, double, cross-shaped |
| Census town | ≥5,000 people, density ≥**400**/km², ≥**75%** male workers non-farm |
| Statutory town | municipality, corporation, **cantonment board**, notified area |
| Size classes | I ≥1 lakh, II **50,000**–99,999, III 20,000+, IV 10,000+, V 5,000+, **Class VI** <5,000 |
| Urban agglomeration | town + **outgrowths** / adjoining towns |
| Conurbation | **Patrick Geddes** (1915): merged cities |
| Megalopolis | Jean **Gottmann** (1957): Boston–Washington |
| Primate city | **Mark Jefferson** (1939) |
| Central place theory | Walter **Christaller** (1933), hexagonal market areas |
| Rank-size rule | G.K. **Zipf**: nth city = 1/n of the largest |
| Concentric zones | E.W. **Burgess** (1925) |

**Towns by function**

| Function | Examples |
|---|---|
| Administrative | **Chandigarh** (**Le Corbusier**), Bhubaneswar, **Gandhinagar**, Dispur |
| Industrial | **Jamshedpur**, **Bhilai**, Salem, Coimbatore |
| Mining | Dhanbad, Jharia, **Raniganj**, **Digboi** |
| Garrison | **Mhow**, Ambala, Jalandhar, **Babina**, Udhampur |
| Religious / cultural | Varanasi, Mathura, Amritsar, **Puri**, **Ajmer**, Tirupati |
| Tourist | Shimla, **Mussoorie**, Nainital, Ooty, **Mount Abu** |
| Transport | ports **Kandla**, Kochi, Visakhapatnam; junctions **Itarsi**, Mughal Sarai |
| Educational | Roorkee, Aligarh, **Pilani**, **Manipal** |
| Historical classes | ancient Varanasi, Patna, **Madurai**; **medieval** Delhi, Hyderabad, Jaipur; colonial Surat, Goa, Puducherry |

**Don't confuse**
Compact = plains; dispersed = hills (Meghalaya, Kerala). Census town = qualifies by criteria; statutory town = notified by law. Geddes = conurbation; Gottmann = megalopolis; Jefferson = primate city; Christaller = central place; Zipf = rank-size.

**TL;DR**
- Rural: compact (Punjab), semi-clustered (Gujarat), hamleted (panna/dhani), dispersed (Meghalaya, Kerala).
- Census town: 5,000 / 400 per km² / 75% non-farm; statutory town: municipal body.
- Terms: Geddes, Gottmann, Jefferson, Christaller, Zipf, Burgess; towns by function: Chandigarh, Jamshedpur, Digboi, Mhow.
keyPoints: Compact settlements dominate the fertile plains; dispersed settlements the hills of Meghalaya, Uttarakhand and Kerala.
Hamleted villages split into units called panna, para, palli, nagla or dhani.
A census town needs 5,000 people, density of 400 per km² and 75% of male main workers outside farming.
Patrick Geddes coined "conurbation"; Jean Gottmann "megalopolis"; Mark Jefferson the "primate city".
Chandigarh (Le Corbusier) is an administrative town; Mhow a garrison town; Digboi an oil-mining town.

### Tribes of India — State, PVTGs and Distinctive Practices

**In one line**
Beyond the classic traps, tribe questions pair a tribe with a state or with a practice (shifting cultivation, matriliny, transhumance, art).

**The story**
India notifies about **705** ST communities. PVTGs were first identified in 1975 (as PTGs) on the **Dhebar** Commission's advice and renamed in **2006**; **PM-JANMAN** (2023) targets the 75 PVTGs. Tribal areas are governed under the Fifth Schedule (most states) or the **Sixth Schedule** (Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram); **PESA** (1996) extends panchayats to Fifth Schedule areas. B.S. **Guha** classified Indians into six races — **Negrito**, Proto-Australoid, Mongoloid, Mediterranean, Western Brachycephals and Nordic.

| Tribe | Where / known for |
|---|---|
| **Bhil** | Rajasthan–MP–Gujarat |
| **Mina** | Largest ST of Rajasthan |
| **Oraon** | Chotanagpur plateau, Jharkhand |
| **Santhal** | Largest tribe of Jharkhand |
| **Baiga** | Bewar shifting cultivation, MP |

items.title: Urbanisation Trend, Slums, Sex-Ratio History and Ageing
items.body:
### Urbanisation Trend, Slums, Sex-Ratio History and Ageing

**In one line**
India urbanised slowly — from about a tenth of its people in 1901 to nearly a third in 2011 — and the 2011 census marked a turning point.

**The story**
The urban share rose from **10.8**% (1901) to 17.3% (1951), **27.8**% (2001) and 31.2% (2011). In 2001–11, for the **first time since 1921**, the absolute increase in urban population exceeded that in rural population; urban numbers grew **31.8**% against **12.2**% for rural. About **6.5 crore** people lived in **slum**s (about 17% of the urban population), Maharashtra having the most and Mumbai's **Dharavi** being among Asia's largest. **Counter-urbanisation** is the drift from cities to villages or small towns, **suburbanisation** the growth of a city's edge; **Over-urbanisation** is urban growth outrunning jobs and services, and **pseudo-urbanisation** is growth driven by rural push rather than urban pull. A **satellite town** such as **Navi Mumbai** or Noida absorbs a big city's overflow.

**Sex ratio and literacy over time:** the sex ratio was **972** in 1901, fell to its lowest, **927**, in 1991, and recovered to 943 in 2011. Literacy was only **18.3**% in 1951.

**Ageing and health:** the **India Ageing Report** 2023 (UNFPA) projects the elderly share to rise from about 10.5% (2022) to about **20.8**% by 2050. Census 2011 counted about **2.68 crore** persons with disabilities; life expectancy is about **70 years**.

**Don't confuse**
Lowest sex ratio was 927 in 1991 (not 2001). 2011 = first decade since 1921 in which urban absolute increase beat rural.

**TL;DR**
- Urban share 10.8% (1901) → 31.2% (2011); urban increase beat rural in 2001–11.
- Slums 6.5 crore (Maharashtra most); terms counter-, over-, pseudo-, sub-urbanisation.
- Sex ratio 972 (1901) → 927 (1991) → 943 (2011); literacy 18.3% (1951); elderly to 20.8% by 2050.
keyPoints: India's urban share rose from 10.8% in 1901 to 31.2% in 2011.
In 2001–11 the absolute urban increase exceeded the rural increase for the first time since 1921.
Census 2011 counted about 6.5 crore slum dwellers, the most in Maharashtra.
India's sex ratio fell from 972 (1901) to its lowest, 927 (1991), before rising to 943 (2011).
The India Ageing Report 2023 projects the elderly share to reach about 20.8% by 2050.

items.title: Peoples and Tribes of the World
items.body:
### Peoples and Tribes of the World

**In one line**
A world-peoples question pairs a people with its homeland and way of life; learn them alongside the Bushmen, Pygmies, Masai and Bedouin already listed.

**The story**
Peoples adapt to their environments: Arctic herders follow reindeer, desert peoples move with water and pasture, forest hunters live off the canopy, and grassland peoples ride and herd.

| People | Homeland / way of life |
|---|---|
| **Ainu** | Hokkaido, Japan |
| **Yakuts** | Lena basin, Siberia |
| **Samoyeds and Chukchi** | Reindeer herders of the Siberian tundra |
| **Berbers** | Atlas mountains, North Africa |
| **Zulu** | KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa |
| **Hottentots (Khoikhoi)** | Pastoralists of Namibia |
| **Semang** | Forests of the Malay Peninsula |
| **Veddas** | Indigenous people of Sri Lanka |
| **Papuans** | New Guinea |
| **Igorot** | Rice-terrace farmers of the Philippines |
| **Gauchos** | Cowboys of the Argentine Pampas |
| **Kazakhs** | Nomads of the Kazakh steppes |
| **Bantu** | Central and southern Africa |

**Don't confuse**
Ainu = Japan (Hokkaido); Yakuts = Siberia; Veddas = Sri Lanka; Semang = Malaysia; Gauchos = Argentina (Pampas) — not Brazil.

**TL;DR**
- Asia: Ainu (Hokkaido), Yakuts (Siberia), Samoyeds/Chukchi (tundra), Semang (Malaya), Veddas (Sri Lanka), Igorot (Philippines), Kazakhs (steppes).
- Africa: Berbers (Atlas), Zulu (South Africa), Hottentots (Namibia), Bantu (central–south); Americas: Gauchos (Pampas).
keyPoints: The Ainu are the indigenous people of Hokkaido, Japan; the Yakuts live in Siberia.
The Berbers live in the Atlas region of North Africa; the Zulu in South Africa.
The Veddas are the indigenous people of Sri Lanka; the Semang of the Malay Peninsula.
Gauchos are the cowboys of the Argentine Pampas.

items.title: For Mains — Social Geography of Andhra Pradesh and India
items.body:
**In one line:** For Mains (Paper-II, General Studies - social/human geography of India and AP), population is asked as a development question: how India's and AP's demographic trends create both opportunities (the dividend) and challenges (ageing, migration, tribal vulnerability).

This note serves syllabus clause **M2-13** (social geography — population, habitations, density, caste/tribe/religion, migration). Convert the Prelims numbers into argument.

## Dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Trends | Falling growth, changing age structure, uneven density, rising urbanisation |
| Opportunities | Demographic dividend, skilling, female workforce |
| Challenges | Jobless growth, ageing (south), migration-driven slums, tribal displacement, declining child sex ratio |
| Way forward | Education and health investment, planned polycentric urbanisation, FRA/PESA for tribes |

## Data points to quote

- Working-age (15-59) share rose to 63% (2011); dividend window to about 2055.
- Urbanisation 31.2% (2011); rural-to-rural is the largest internal stream, marriage-driven for women.
- 75 PVTGs across 18 states and 1 UT; undivided AP had 12; Chenchu (Nallamala) and Yanadi (largest AP ST).
- AP sex ratio 997 (above national 943) but literacy about 67% (below national 74%); near-replacement TFR 1.7 (NFHS-5).
- Census 2027: first digital census, caste enumeration (first since 1931), feeds delimitation.

## AP angle

AP is a demographic 'early mover': near-replacement fertility and an ageing profile like other southern states mean its dividend window is **narrower and closing sooner** than north India's. Pair this with coastal urbanisation around Visakhapatnam, Rayalaseema out-migration, and the welfare of Eastern-Ghats tribes under the Forest Rights Act and PESA.

## Use in answers

- Example: cite AP's TFR 1.7 and ageing to argue for urgent skilling before the dividend fades.
- Quote: 'demographic dividend can become a demographic liability' without jobs and human capital.
- Diagram idea: a population pyramid narrowing at the base (falling 0-14 share) to show the transition and the closing window.
keyPoints: Mains (Paper-II, clause M2-13) asks population as a development question, not a fact list.
Frame along trends, opportunities (dividend), challenges (ageing, migration, tribal vulnerability) and way forward.
Quote working-age 63% (2011), urbanisation 31.2%, 75 PVTGs, AP sex ratio 997 vs literacy 67%, TFR 1.7, Census 2027.
Core AP angle: an early-transition state whose dividend window closes sooner, with coastal urbanisation and tribal welfare issues.
Use the 'dividend to liability' quote and a narrowing population pyramid as a diagram.
